\subsection{Cross-Model Comparison}
\label{sec:cross_model}

We compare Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct under four input conditions (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}).

\begin{table}[t]

\toprule

\midrule

VOTA & 99.41\% & 84.45\% & 14.96pp \\
VOTA\_no\_ae & 99.41\%$^\S$ & --- & --- \\
full\_trace & 81.76\% & 79.16\% & 2.60pp \\
no\_trace & 75.13\% & 73.36\% & 1.77pp \\
\midrule
Majority baseline & 71.51\% & 71.51\% & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\label{tab:cross_model}
\end{table}

Under \texttt{exception\_only}, Qwen achieves 99.83\% $\pm$ 0.00 across three seeds, while DeepSeek achieves 99.33\% on 2/3 seeds (seed 123 yields 91.09\% due to LoRA initialization sensitivity).

Verdict prediction is fundamentally a fault detection task: the model must determine whether execution deviated from expected behavior.
Exception events are the most explicit signal of such deviation---structured diagnostic moments that encode the nature and location of a fault.

Execution traces---line-by-line records of a program's runtime behavior---have emerged as a promising input modality for code language models.
Recent work has explored trace-augmented training for code generation \citep{chen2025tracepile}, execution-aware pretraining \citep{ding2024traced}, trace-based code understanding \citep{wang2025dcsh}, and self-training on trace chain-of-thought \citep{ni2024next}.
Yet a fundamental question remains open: \emph{which components of an execution trace actually matter?}

\citet{wang2025dcsh} found that no single trace representation consistently outperforms others on generation-oriented tasks, concluding that the utility of execution traces is task- and format-dependent.
However, their study focused on code generation and repair---tasks that require the model to simulate or reconstruct execution semantics.
\emph{Verdict prediction}---classifying whether a test passes or fails---is a fundamentally different task type: it is a fault detection problem, not a generation problem.
Whether the same trace components matter for fault detection as for generation is unknown.

We present the first systematic study of what trace components drive verdict prediction performance.
Using 591 problems from HumanEval \citep{chen2021evaluating} and MBPP-sanitized \citep{austin2021program} with model-generated solutions and execution traces, we decompose a multi-component trace representation (VOTA: exception events + assertion-point comparisons + loop compression) into individual components and evaluate each in isolation across four models spanning 1.5B--13B parameters and three architecture families: Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, Qwen-2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct, DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B-Instruct, and CodeLlama-13B-Instruct-hf.

Our results reveal a striking finding: \textbf{exception events alone achieve $\geq$99.33\% accuracy on all four models regardless of scale (1.5B--13B), with three of four reaching the 99.83\% ceiling.}
This scale invariance contrasts sharply with the no-trace baseline, which shows strict scale monotonicity: 67.31\% (1.5B) $<$ 73.36\% (6.7B) $<$ 75.13\% (7B) $<$ 76.50\% (13B), confirming that information quality dominates model scale.
VOTA results are more variable across models: Qwen-1.5B (99.58\%) and CodeLlama-13B (98.57\%) maintain high accuracy, while DeepSeek collapses to 84.45\%.
Post-hoc analysis reveals the mechanism for the DeepSeek VOTA collapse: the DeepSeek tokenizer produces longer sequences than Qwen for identical inputs, causing 91.7\% of VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window; the training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates the trace content, so the model trains on incomplete diagnostic information.

These results reframe verdict prediction as fault detection: the minimal sufficient signal is the exception event, a compact structured diagnostic moment that models of all scales can interpret without deep trace reasoning.
We further decompose the gap between full trace and VOTA into two mechanisms---\emph{gradient dilution} (26\% of the gap) and \emph{information overload} (74\%)---showing that the primary bottleneck is not training signal quality but the presence of irrelevant trace content.

We note that the finding that exception events dominate verdict prediction is not itself surprising---exceptions are, by definition, fault indicators.
The novelty lies in four less obvious results: (1)~adding more trace information actively \emph{hurts} performance (VOTA $<$ \texttt{exception\_only}), (2)~we quantify \emph{why} through a 26/74 gradient-dilution/information-overload decomposition, (3)~the VOTA cross-model gap is confounded by tokenizer-driven trace truncation: the DeepSeek tokenizer causes the majority of VOTA training samples to exceed the context window (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}), truncating diagnostic trace content while preserving the verdict label, and (4)~exception events exhibit complete scale invariance (1.5B--13B) while no-trace accuracy is strictly scale-monotonic, demonstrating that information quality dominates model capacity.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Exception signal transfer and scale invariance}: We show that exception events alone achieve $\geq$99.33\% on all four models regardless of scale (1.5B--13B), with three of four reaching the 99.83\% ceiling, while the no-trace baseline shows strict scale monotonicity (67.31\%--76.50\%); information quality dominates model scale (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}, \S\ref{sec:cross_scale}).

\item \textbf{Two-tier diagnostic hierarchy}: Component ablation reveals that Tier~1 signals (exception events, assertion points) individually achieve ${\geq}$99.8\% accuracy while Tier~2 signals (loop compression) reach only 85.6\% (\S\ref{sec:ablation}).
